caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Burundi's debt was transformed by HIPC/MDRI relief: from a crushing 130.3% of GDP in 2006, completion-point relief brought it down to 25.7% by 2009. Since then it has crept back up through fiscal deficits and donor withdrawal after the 2015 crisis, reaching 69.8% in 2022 before easing to a projected 41.2% in 2025 as the denominator recovered. The debt is mostly concessional and domestic, so near-term solvency is not the issue; the issue is that borrowing has financed consumption and the security apparatus rather than productive investment, while arrears to the private sector accumulate.
inflation_management: Burundi's inflation history is one of repeated loss of control. It ran at 24.4% in 2008 during the global food-fuel crisis, then moderated to single digits through the early 2010s, even turning to deflation in 2018 (-2.8%) and 2019 (-0.8%). The current crisis is worse: a severe foreign-exchange shortage, monetized deficits, and a collapsing parallel exchange rate pushed inflation to 18.9% in 2022, 27.1% in 2023, 20.2% in 2024, and a series high of 34.2% projected for 2025. The central bank has devalued the franc in steps but remains far from a market-clearing rate, so inflation expectations are unanchored and basic goods are chronically scarce.

key_events.event: HIPC completion-point debt relief cut public debt from 130.3% (2006) to 25.7% of GDP.
President Nkurunziza's bid for a third term triggered protests, a failed coup, and a crackdown; donors suspended direct budget support, deepening the forex crisis.
Nkurunziza died in office; Evariste Ndayishimiye succeeded him, with modest diplomatic re-engagement.
Ukraine war and forex shortages pushed inflation to 27.1%; the central bank devalued the franc.
Inflation projected at 34.2%, the series high, amid continued parallel-market depreciation and goods shortages.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued stagflation: without a credible exchange-rate adjustment and restored donor relations, inflation will stay high and growth too low to reduce poverty. Upside depends on genuine forex liberalization and agricultural recovery; downside is a full-blown currency crisis. Uncertainty is high: the political system is stable but closed, and economic data quality is weak, so even the direction of travel is hard to verify.
